n: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH)

faq.a: Excess ADH causes water retention without sodium gain, expanding total body water but not extracellular fluid volume.
faq.q: Why is the patient euvolemic despite hyponatraemia?

faq.a: Yes; CNS infections, drugs, and other tumours can also trigger inappropriate ADH release.
faq.q: Can SIADH occur without lung disease?

faq.a: No; raising Na⁺ >8‑10 mmol/L in 24 h risks osmotic demyelination, so correct slowly.
faq.q: Is rapid correction of sodium safe?

exam: A 6‑year‑old with pneumonia develops confusion and Na⁺ 122 mmol/L. What is the next immediate step? — Assess volume status, restrict free water, and begin cautious hypertonic saline if neurologic symptoms are present.
How does SIADH differ from hypovolaemic hyponatraemia on urine studies? — SIADH shows urine Na⁺ >30 mmol/L and concentrated urine; hypovolaemia usually has low urine Na⁺ and variable osmolality.

Why is fluid restriction preferred over diuretics in most paediatric SIADH cases? — It limits free water intake without risking further electrolyte loss; diuretics may worsen hyponatraemia if not carefully managed.
A child on carbamazepine presents with mild hyponatraemia. What should you do? — Review medication, consider stopping carbamazepine, and implement fluid restriction while monitoring Na⁺.
What are the dangers of giving normal saline to a patient with SIADH? — It adds sodium but also free water, potentially worsening hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema.
Explain why osmotic demyelination syndrome is a concern when treating severe SIADH. — Over‑rapid rise in serum Na⁺ creates an osmotic gradient that damages myelin in the central pons.
Which tropical infection is a common cause of SIADH in East Africa and how would you confirm it? — Cerebral malaria; confirm with thick blood smear and treat promptly.
When is hypertonic saline indicated in paediatric SIADH? — In severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (Na⁺ <125 mmol/L with seizures or coma) after ensuring airway protection.
ai.title: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH)
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: SIADH is a disorder of water balance causing euvolemic hyponatraemia with low plasma osmolality. It is common in children with infections, malignancy or drug exposure, especially in low‑resource settings where diagnostics are limited.

b: Serum Na⁺ < 135 mmol/L
Serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg (inappropriately concentrated)
Urine Na⁺ > 30 mmol/L
Absence of edema, hypotension, or signs of volume depletion
sections.p: SIADH is characterised by excess ADH activity leading to water retention, dilutional hyponatraemia and low plasma osmolality, while extracellular fluid volume remains normal.

t.b: Confirms hyponatraemia and hypo‑osmolar state; low values support SIADH
Shows kidneys are concentrating urine despite low plasma osmolality; values >100 mOsm/kg and >30 mmol/L indicate inappropriate ADH
Distinguishes euvolemic SIADH from hypovolaemic or hypervolemic hyponatraemia

b: Mild: Na 130‑134 mmol/L, asymptomatic
Moderate: Na 125‑129 mmol/L, nausea, headache, mild confusion
Severe: Na <125 mmol/L, seizures, coma, respiratory arrest
sections.p: Severity is graded by serum sodium level and symptom burden, guiding urgency of treatment.

b: Pulmonary infections (pneumonia, TB, malaria‑related lung disease)
Central nervous system infections (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria)
Medications: carbamazepine, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Malignancy: small‑cell lung carcinoma, neuroblastoma, lymphoma
Post‑operative stress or pain
Herbal remedies containing unknown sympathomimetics
sections.p: In children, the most common triggers are infections and drugs; malignancy is rarer but important.

b: Nausea, vomiting
Headache, lethargy, irritability
Seizures or altered consciousness in severe cases
No peripheral oedema, normal blood pressure
sections.p: Children often present with nonspecific neurological symptoms due to cerebral oedema, while appearing clinically euvolemic.
Focus on confirming hyponatraemia, assessing volume status and identifying the underlying trigger.

t.b: Shows low Na⁺, low osmolality; guides severity
Urine Na⁺ >30 mmol/L and osmolality >100 mOsm/kg support SIADH
Detects pulmonary infection or tumour; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture and treat presumptively
Identifies CNS infection as a cause

b: Seizures or sudden loss of consciousness
Respiratory arrest from brainstem compression
Persistent hyponatraemia despite fluid restriction
sections.p: Rapid fall in sodium can cause cerebral oedema and death.

b: Identify and treat infection or stop offending drug
Fluid restriction to 800‑1000 mL/24 h (or <50 % of maintenance) if tolerated
Oral salt tablets or hypertonic saline (3 % NaCl) for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; give slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination
Vaptans (e.g., tolvaptan) are rarely available; avoid in low‑resource settings
Monitor serum Na⁺ every 4‑6 h initially
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, restrict free water, and use pharmacologic agents when needed.

b: Re‑measure serum Na⁺ and osmolality after 24 h and before discharge
Educate caregivers on fluid restriction and medication risks
Schedule follow‑up within 1‑2 weeks to reassess volume status and Na⁺
sections.p: Regular monitoring after acute correction prevents relapse and detects chronic causes.

b: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (e.g., diarrhoea, vomiting)
Hypervolemic hyponatraemia (e.g., heart failure, nephrotic syndrome)
Primary polydipsia (excessive water intake)
sections.p: Conditions that also cause hyponatraemia but differ in volume status or pathophysiology.

b: Urine osmolality can be low early in the course, giving a false‑negative
Serum cortisol not measured may miss adrenal insufficiency masquerading as SIADH
sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite underlying SIADH.

whenToSeekHelp: Seizures, coma, or rapid decline in mental status
Failure of sodium to rise with appropriate therapy
